Celldex Presents Positive First-in-Human Results from Phase 1 Study of Novel Bispecific CDX-622 at the European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology Annual Meeting June 14, 2026 05:15 ET | Source: Celldex Therapeutics, Inc. Follow Celldex Therapeutics, Inc. Share CDX-622 is a novel, bispecific antibody combining mast cell depletion and TSLP inhibition, two independent pathways contributing to multiple I&I diseases CDX-622 targets the soluble form of stem cell factor (SCF), depleting mast cells without measurably impacting other KIT functions Rapid, profound, dose-dependent, and durable reductions in serum tryptase observed Well-tolerated at all dose levels First company to demonstrate that neutralizing soluble SCF can selectively inhibit KIT signaling in mast cells HAMPTON, N.J., June  14, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Celldex (NASDAQ:CLDX) today presented positive results from the Phase 1 healthy participant study of CDX-622, a novel, bispecific antibody that targets soluble SCF and TSLP, at the European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (EAACI) Annual Meeting in Istanbul, Türkiye. Data demonstrated that CDX-622 induced rapid, durable, dose-dependent reductions in serum tryptase, indicative of mast cell depletion, and was well-tolerated at all dose levels. Building on Celldex’s leadership in mast cell science, the data also demonstrated that neutralizing soluble stem cell factor (SCF) enables the potential for meaningful mast cell inhibition and depletion without impacting other KIT-dependent functions. CDX-622 is currently being studied in a Phase 1b proof of mechanism study in mild to moderate asthma to assess the impact of dual neutralization of SCF and TSLP. “Celldex continues to drive groundbreaking science and is the first company to directly demonstrate that neutralizing soluble stem cell factor can selectively inhibit KIT signaling in mast cells, a historically challenging target,” said Tibor Keler, Ph.D., Co-founder, Executive Vice President and Chief Scientific Officer at Celldex. “Importantly, the approach of targeting soluble SCF provides a promising anchor mechanism enabling the development of a robust portfolio of bispecific candidates designed to overcome the heterogeneity inherent in the pathophysiology of many inflammatory diseases. Today’s results from CDX-622 highlight the potential of this approach and we look forward to initiating additional proof of concept studies in multiple indications where both mast cells and TSLP play a pathogenic role, focusing next on allergic rhinitis and food allergy.” “Mast cell targeting strategies are rapidly emerging as powerful therapeutic approaches in inflammatory diseases. Leveraging our expertise in antibody drug development, and building on our success with barzolvolimab, Celldex is committed to driving innovation across the field of mast cell science to bring our leading science to additional patient populations that could benefit from our medicines,” said  Anthony Marucci, Co-Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer at Celldex. “Barzolvolimab and CDX-622 target mast cells through two distinct, highly synergistic platform approaches. Together, these novel candidates build a powerful foundation for a broad portfolio of therapeutics targeting a wide range of inflammatory diseases where mast cells are implicated. We look forward to sharing more about our growing pipeline in the future.” Data Summary: CDX-622 is a uniquely engineered novel bispecific antibody that targets soluble SCF and alarmin thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), two critical pathways that may contribute to the pathology of several allergic and inflammatory disorders with significant unmet medical need. Combined neutralization of SCF and TSLP with CDX-622 is expected to simultaneously reduce tissue mast cells and inhibit Type 2 inflammatory responses, allowing for a complementary dual mechanism approach that may overcome the heterogeneity inherent in the pathophysiology of many inflammatory disorders. CDX-622 has been engineered to disable effector function (AQQ) and enhance half-life (YTE). Rapid, profound, dose-dependent, and durable reductions in serum tryptase were observed, indicative of tissue mast cell inhibition and depletion. Tryptase decreases were comparable to KIT-targeting following multiple doses. Biopsy data were consistent with greater impact on mucosal mast cells than skin mast cells. CDX-622 exhibited monoclonal antibody-like pharmacokinetics, with extended half-life and good exposure with subcutaneous administration, consistent with good bioavailability. There was no evidence of immunogenicity at any dose. CDX-622 was well-tolerated in all study parts and at all dose levels. There were no dose-limiting toxicities or related serious adverse events. The most commonly reported adverse event across the study was Grade 1 headache. There were no changes in hair or skin pigmentation. There was no meaningful impact on hematologic parameters. Additionally, in June, Celldex presented new non-human primate data at the European Mast Cell and Basophil Research Network (EMBRN) that validates the approach of targeting soluble SCF to deplete mast cells. The preclinical study evaluated antibodies either targeting soluble SCF or both soluble and the membrane form of SCF. The data showed that targeting soluble SCF effectively depleted mast cells in a manner similar to targeting membrane SCF, but without measurable effect on spermatogenesis or melanogenesis in non-human primates. Results support that combined TSLP neutralization and mast cell depletion with CDX-622 may result in broad efficacy in inflammatory diseases where both pathways play a pathogenic role. About the Phase 1 Study The Phase 1 trial was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose escalation study designed to assess the safety, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and immunogenicity of single ascending doses (Part 1) and multiple ascending doses (Part 2) of CDX-622 in healthy participants. The study also included a single ascending dose of CDX-622 administered subcutaneously (Part 3). 32 participants were enrolled in Part 1 across 4 cohorts (8 participants per cohort; n=6 CDX-622, n=2 placebo) and received single ascending intravenous doses of CDX-622 (0.3, 1.0, 3.0 and 9.0 mg/kg) and were observed over a 12-week period. 24 participants were enrolled in Part 2 across 3 cohorts (8 participants per cohort; n=6 CDX-622, n=2 placebo) and received multiple ascending intravenous doses of CDX-622 (1.0, 3.0, and 9.0 mg/kg at weeks 2, 4, and 6) and were observed for 18 weeks. 24 participants were enrolled in Part 3 across 3 cohorts (8 participants per cohort; n=6 CDX-622, n=2 placebo) and received single ascending subcutaneous doses of CDX-622 (290, 580, and 870 mg) and were observed for 12 weeks. Data from Part 1 were previously presented in October 2025. About 622: CDX-622 is a bispecific antibody that targets two complementary, clinically validated pathways that drive chronic inflammation, potently neutralizing the alarmin thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) and depleting mast cells via stem cell factor (SCF) starvation. SCF activation of the KIT receptor is required for mast cell survival and plays a key role in their activation, maturation and tissue recruitment. Combined neutralization of SCF and TSLP with CDX-622 is expected to simultaneously reduce tissue mast cells and inhibit Type 2 inflammatory responses to potentially offer enhanced therapeutic benefit in inflammatory and fibrotic disorders. About Barzolvolimab: Barzolvolimab is a humanized monoclonal antibody with a novel mechanism of action that targets mast cells by binding with high specificity to a unique part of the KIT receptor and potently inhibiting its activity. The KIT receptor is abundantly expressed by mast cells and critical for their function and survival. Mast cells are drivers of inflammatory responses such as hypersensitivity and allergic reactions and, in certain inflammatory diseases, such as chronic urticarias, mast cell activation plays a central role in the onset and progression of the disease. Based on data from robust, randomized, placebo controlled Phase 2 studies, barzolvolimab has significant potential as a first-in-class and best-in-disease treatment option for patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), cold urticaria (ColdU) and symptomatic dermographism (SD). Barzolvolimab is currently being studied in Phase 3 studies in CSU and ColdU/SD and Phase 2 studies in prurigo nodularis (PN) and atopic dermatitis (AD), with additional indications planned for the future. About Celldex Celldex is pioneering new horizons in immunology to deliver life-changing therapies. We are relentless in our pursuit of novel antibody-based treatments that engage the human immune system and directly affect critical pathways to improve the lives of patients with allergic, inflammatory and autoimmune disorders. Visit www.celldex.com . Back to Healio Save Share LinkedIn Facebook X (Twitter) Bluesky Threads Email Copy Link Key takeaways: The addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to first-line R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% for patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said. “The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. Perspective Back to Top Krish Patel, MD Krish Patel, MD For more than 2 decades, R-CHOP has been the global standard of care for newly diagnosed patients with DLBCL, leading to cure in about 60% of patients. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. Krish Patel, MD SCRI Oncology Partners Sarah Cannon Research Institute Disclosures: Patel reports research funding to his institution from, consulting/advisory roles with or speakers bureau roles with AbbVie, AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Genentech, Genmab, Janssen, Kite Pharma, Merck, Pfizer, Sanofi and other companies. Perspective Back to Top Tycel Phillips, MD Tycel Phillips, MD Improving response and curability remains paramount for management of patients with first-line DLBCL, despite improvement of salvage options. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Tycel Phillips, MD City of Hope Disclosures: Phillips reports research support from, advisory board roles with or scientific board roles with AbbVie, Adaptive, ADC Therapeutics, AstraZeneca, BeOne Medicines, Bristol Myers Squibb, Caribou, Eli Lilly & Co., Epizyme, Genentech, Genmab, Gilead Sciences, Incyte, Janssen/Johnson & Johnson, Kite Pharma, Legend Biotech, Merck, Pfizer, Pharmacyclics, Seagen and Sobi. The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said. “The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. That information hopefully will help answer the question about where tafasitamab belongs. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas.

All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment.
Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles.
PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints.
‘Good chance’ for cure
Median follow-up reached 35.2 months.
The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed.
The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin.
Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%).
“Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.”
Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%).
An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival.
“We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said.
‘Manageable’ toxicities
The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events.
Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%).
More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%).
Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles.
“The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.”
Evolving treatment landscape
The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment.
The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting.
The New England Journal of Medicine
Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment.
The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL.
epcoritamab
The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said.
“The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out.
“Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.”

Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Skip to content Suggested Topics: Home Best in Biotech Eight oncology deals in 2026 spotlight where industry leaders are betting big Photo credits: Cytonn Photography (Unsplash) Newsletter Signup - Under Article / In Page " * " indicates required fields Biotech partnerships play a critical role in driving innovation through the sharing of knowledge, expertise, and resources, and are particularly important in bridging the gap between early-stage research and commercial development. As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. In this article, we look at eight of the biggest oncology deals that have been made so far in 2026. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China. AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer. Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S. Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership. Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%. VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index. The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales. Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials. Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales. This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die. These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise. Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer. Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization. Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement. Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top
Back to Top
In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide.
announced
Chinese biotech company
The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS.
The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs.
Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion.
Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top
In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines.
entered into
The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.”
The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development.
Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top
The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies.
The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China.

The financial terms of the deal included a $350 million upfront payment for Innovent, with the company also eligible to receive up to approximately $8.5 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments.
AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top
At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors.
PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs.
In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer.
Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory.
BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top
In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis.
formed
trispecific antibody
Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S.
Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales.
Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top
February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership.
enter into
T-cell engager
Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%.
survival rate
VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index.
The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales.
Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top
In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials.
licensing
Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales.
This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die.
acquired
These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise.
Gilead’s pipeline strategy
Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top
In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer.
entering into
degrader-antibody conjugate modality
Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization.
Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement.

articles.title: WuXi Biologics gets South Korean GMP certification for bispecific antibody
articles.text:
Industry News WuXi Biologics gets South Korean GMP certification for bispecific antibody The certification enables end-to-end commercial manufacturing across drug substance, fill-finish, and packaging for complex biologics targeting oncology indications. April 24, 2026 2 min read WuXi Biologics, a global contract research, development, and manufacturing organization (CRDMO), announced that three manufacturing facilities in Wuxi, China, have received Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) certification from South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety, enabling commercial manufacturing of a bispecific antibody for biliary tract cancer. The certification covers the company’s Drug Substance Facility 5, Drug Product Facility 2, and Drug Product Packaging Center, supporting integrated capabilities from drug substance manufacturing through fill-finish and packaging. Earlier this month, the company launched an automated fill-finish system to reduce manual intervention and improve consistency in cell therapy manufacturing workflows, and a Chinese hamster ovary (CHO)-based platform designed to compress development timelines and improve process consistency for biologics and biosimilar manufacturers. Armin Spura, CEO of BioDuro, said in a statement that combining BioDuro’s integrated discovery and development capabilities with CTI’s GLP toxicology and bioanalytical expertise is intended to help clients advance innovative programs with greater speed and efficiency. Tony Liu, general manager of CTI Biotechnology, said in a statement the collaboration will provide clients worldwide with a more complete and efficient integrated preclinical development solution. The agreement builds on BioDuro’s recent efforts to expand its development and manufacturing network. Last month, the company announced a joint venture in Taiwan to increase API manufacturing capacity , integrating early-stage development capabilities with commercial-scale GMP production to support clinical through commercial supply. CordenPharma said both inspections resulted in zero observations, confirming the site’s GMP framework and its ability to manage complex, highly potent manufacturing processes. The company said the outcome supports its containment strategies and operational controls for handling highly potent compounds. The Plankstadt facility’s inspection results come as the company continues to expand its global manufacturing and development footprint. Last month, CordenPharma announced an expansion of its peptide development capabilities in Boulder, Colorado, adding laboratory space to support process development and analytical services alongside its existing peptide API manufacturing operations. The company said the expanded capabilities are intended to improve alignment between development and manufacturing activities and support growing outsourcing demand across its global network. articles.title: Akeso and Summit's ivonescimab extends survival in squamous cell lung cancer
articles.text:
Skip to Main Content
STAT Plus Biotech Akeso and Summit’s ivonescimab extends survival in squamous cell lung cancer ‘Two drugs in one’ candidate, developed in China, is a highlight at ASCO Manage alerts for this article Email this article Share this article By Matthew Herper May 31, 2026 Senior Writer, Medicine, Editorial Director of Events Matthew Herper matthew.herper@statnews.com Matthew Herper covers medical innovation — both its promise and its perils. Get email alerts for Matthew Herper Signed up for email alerts Remove email alerts Subscribe or log in to STAT+ to unlock email alerts CHICAGO — Ivonescimab, a drug that combines the activity of two of the best-selling cancer medicines, reduced the risk of death in patients with squamous non-small cell lung cancer by 34% compared to a standard treatment in a clinical trial conducted entirely in China by the drug’s developer, Akeso, according to data presented Sunday. The result, oncologists say, exceeded their expectations, and it appears it could generate optimism for the drug, which is being developed outside China by Summit Therapeutics. But the data also are likely to fuel debate on issues like the role of China in drug development and the future of cancer treatments. The results were presented here at the annual meeting of the American Society of Clinical Oncology and are being published simultaneously in The Lancet . Advertisement Robert Duggan, Summit’s co-CEO and chairman, said that the data mean the company has “a very valuable business with a very valuable product that is in its early stages.” Akeso had no comment for this story.
